title: Man Quizzes Daughter For Her Driving Test. Then He Asks Her What Color Yield Signs Are: 'Is This A Mandela Effect?'
excerpt: A viral video has drivers questioning the color of yield signs, revealing why so many people still picture them as yellow.
content:
Cue the final "Jeopardy!" countdown music and riddle me this: What is the primary color of a yield sign on the road? If you’re like a lot of folks, there are suddenly conflicting answers in your head after initially jumping to an answer that seemed certain.

That quandary is the main thrust of a viral TikTok clip from a creator who felt the same confusion while quizzing his daughter to prepare her for her driving skills test.

“We both kind of laughed like, 'This is going to be easy. Yellow, duh,'” he said in the video that's been viewed more than 58,000 times.

Then he reveals the kicker: “She's never seen a yellow yield sign. In fact, most people alive have not seen a yellow yield sign ever in their lifetime. They were all changed in 1971.” To what, you ask? Red and white inverted triangles.

Signs Of The Time

Here’s the thing: Bradshaw and his daughter weren’t completely wrong to jump to yellow and black.

Yellow yield signs were very real. The yield sign was introduced into the national traffic-control manual in 1954 as a downward-pointing triangle with black lettering on a yellow background. It even carried the longer command “YIELD RIGHT OF WAY.”

The red-and-white version came later, with the federal standard changing in 1971, as Bradshaw pointed out. It took a while for the signage change to take hold on roadways across the country, but the design Bradshaw pictured has been obsolete for more than half a century.

That explains why someone old enough to have actually seen one might remember it, but it does considerably less to explain his daughter.

“Why do we all think yellow?” one viewer asked.

'Is This A Mandela Effect?'

That quickly became the unofficial investigation taking place in Bradshaw’s comments section.

“Probably because caution signs are typically yellow,” another viewer offered.

Several others arrived at essentially the same theory from a slightly different direction: traffic lights. A yellow light already tells a driver to exercise caution, so perhaps our brains simply shove “yield” into the same mental bucket.

There’s at least some road-sign logic behind that idea. Under the current federal traffic-sign system, yellow is still overwhelmingly associated with warning signs, while regulatory signs such as yield use red, white, and black.

Other commenters blamed something altogether different.

“Because that color was ingrained into our brains in childhood picture books,” one viewer wrote.

“Kids toys,” another offered.

And then there were commenters pointing out the simplest explanation of all: yield signs actually were yellow for decades.

Drivers Think Yellow Means Caution

There was a practical reason for the color change beyond simply bringing a new color scheme to the nation's road signs. When the federal standard switched in 1971, the new red-and-white yield sign brought the American version closer to the international “give way” symbol already used elsewhere in the world.

The change also helped separate two different kinds of messages drivers receive. Yellow became strongly associated with warnings for things like curves, changing road conditions, and other situations demanding extra attention, while red was reserved for the more direct regulatory commands of stop and yield.

The collective yellow-sign memory among motorists young and old is what’s more curious, but there’s the previously mentioned associative property at play. A yield sign is directing drivers to slow down and be cautious, which feels an awful lot like the behavior we've been trained to associate with yellow traffic lights.

What do you think?

That still leaves the strange generational wrinkle and possible Mandela effect at the center of Bradshaw’s video. His daughter apparently arrived at the same answer despite growing up long after the old signs disappeared from common use.

Bradshaw and his daughter may therefore have reached the same wrong answer by two entirely different routes: one through an old piece of traffic-sign history and the other through a lifetime of seeing yellow used everywhere else to communicate caution and consideration for other motorists.
